content_body:
• Family

Family refers to a group of individuals who are connected by blood, marriage, or strong emotional bonds.

The roles, rights and responsibilities of different family members

Parents

Roles: Caregivers, educators, role models, and providers of emotional and financial support.

Rights: To make decisions in the best interest of their children, including education, healthcare, and upbringing.

Responsibilities: Ensuring the well-being and development of their children, modeling appropriate behavior, and maintaining a safe and nurturing environment.

Children

Roles: Learners, contributors to household chores, and participants in family activities.

Rights: To be cared for, protected, and provided with education and opportunities for personal growth.

Responsibilities: To respect family rules, contribute to household tasks, and engage in their own development and education.

Siblings

Roles: Companions, supporters, and sometimes collaborators in shared responsibilities.

Rights: To be treated with fairness and respect, and to have their own needs and interests considered.

Responsibilities: To support one another, share family responsibilities, and maintain healthy relationships with each other.

Causes of Conflicts and misunderstandings between parents/guardians and children

  • Poor academic Performance.
  • Conflicts can occur if children do not meet behavioral expectations set by their parents, leading to misunderstandings about acceptable conduct.
  • Communication Gaps when Parents and children misinterpret each other’s words or actions due to differing communication style
  • Control Issues Parents may struggle with letting go and giving their children more freedom, leading to tension and disagreement.
  • Punishment as methods of discipline. Children might see punishment as unfair, while parents may view it as necessary for correction.
  • Decisions about college, job choices, or lifestyle can lead to conflicts if parents and children have differing views.
  • Screen Time Limits: Disagreements often arise over the amount of time children spend on devices, including Phone, TV etc
  • Differences in religious beliefs or practices can lead to misunderstandings and disagreements.
  • Financial Issues such as allowance and Spending

Ways in Resolving conflicts or misunderstandings between parents/guardians and children

  • Open and Honest Communication and active Listening. Both parties should listen attentively to each other's perspectives without interrupting.
  • Build Trust and Respect
  • Recognize and validate each other’s feelings, even if you don’t agree with the perspective.
  • Set Aside Time for Discussion.
  • Set and Respect Boundaries and Agree on Rules.
  • Recognize and appreciate each other’s efforts and positive behavior.

Ways to express friendship and love to another person.

  • Express Appreciation Regularly tell the people what you appreciate about them and how much they mean to you.
  • Make an effort to spend time with the people, whether through activities you both enjoy or simply being present.
  • Perform small acts of kindness, such as running an errand for them, helping with a task, or bringing them their favorite treat.
  • Surprise them with something they like or need, such as a book by their favorite author or a favorite snack.
  • Simply being there for someone during challenging times can provide comfort and show you care.
  • Offer encouragement and support for their goals, dreams, and endeavors. Celebrate their achievements and offer a helping hand when needed.
  • Engage in activities that both of you enjoy, such as going to a concert, hiking, or cooking a meal together. Shared experiences can strengthen bonds.
  • Honor their personal space and boundaries. Respect their preferences and individuality.

(Friendship, Love, Romantic relationship and Dating)

Relationships are avenues where adolescents can safely feel and express respect for themselves and others.  .  .  . Types of relationships include;

Friendship: Friendships are an essential part of adolescent development. . . .

Love: Love is a strong feeling of warm personal attachment or deep affection for someone, such as for a parent, child or friend. Love is considered to be positive, with its  representing human , , and —"the unselfish, loyal and benevolent concern for the good of another". Most adolescents misinterpret love as sex, but LOVE IS NOT SEX, neither is sex a component of love.

Romantic relationship: Romantic relationships are often reserved for much matured adults because it is linked in a way adults. It comes along with all the other changes going on during this period - physical, social, and emotional. Adolescents can spend a lot of time thinking about romantic relationships, and this type of relationship can bring many emotional ups and downs for them, which could be very complicated to handle by so doing taking a negative toll on their lives, and distracting them from their education which should be their main focus.

Dating: Otherwise known as courtship, dating is a higher stage of a romantic relationship in which two individuals engage in activities together, most often with the intention of evaluating each other's suitability as a partner in a future  such as marriage. It usually consists of  carried out by the couple either alone or with others.

Infatuation; Refers to an intense but often short-lived passion or admiration for someone, usually characterized by strong feelings of attraction and idealization. Infatuation can involve obsessive thoughts and a heightened focus on the person's physical or superficial traits, often lacking the depth and stability found in more enduring emotional connections.

Sexual Attraction; is a desire for physical intimacy with someone based primarily on sexual desire. It is focused on the physical and sexual aspects of the person rather than emotional or romantic connection. Sexual attraction can exist independently of emotional involvement or a deeper relationship.

Building healthy relationships is an important part of your personal growth and well-being. Here are some tips to help you build healthy relationships:

  • Respect each other: Respect is the foundation of any healthy relationship. .
  • Build trust: Trust is essential in any healthy relationship. .
  • Be supportive: Supporting each other through good times and bad is an important part of building a healthy relationship. .
  • Spend quality time together: Spending quality time together is an important part of building a healthy relationship. .
  • Be willing to compromise: Compromise is essential in any healthy relationship. .
  • Practice forgiveness: Forgiveness is an important part of building a healthy relationship. .
  • Maintain your own identity: Maintaining your own identity outside of the relationship is an important part of building a healthy relationship. .

Remember that building healthy relationships takes time and effort, but it’s worth it in the end.

2.1. KEY DEFINITIONS

What is Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH)

What is Sexual Health

Sexual health is an integral part of overall health, well-being and quality of life. It is a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality, and not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity.

Sexual health requires a positive and respectful approach to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the possibility of having pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free of coercion, discrimination and violence. For sexual health to be attained and maintained, the sexual rights of all people must be respected, protected and fulfilled.

What is Reproductive Health

Reproductive health (RH) implies that people are able to have a responsible, satisfying and safe sex life and that they have the capability to have children and the freedom to decide if, when and how often to do so.

Linking Sexual and Reproductive Health to Rights

  • What are the Rights
  • The right to health care
  • The right to privacy
  • The right to particiapation
  • The right to protection
  • The right to non-discrimination
  • The right to obtain information
  • The right to express opinion
  • The right learning (and education)
  • The right to life and growth to the fullest possible extent
  • .

Description of linkage

  • Enjoyment of SRH is a basic part of the right to enjoy life and health and grow to the fullest possible extent
  • We have the right to protection from sexual abuse, STIs, early marriage, unsafe abortion and undesired pregnancy
  • We have the right to express opinion and feelings of sexuality and we have the right to participation in decisions that concerns us
  • We have the right to knowledge/education/sex education and the right to obtain SRH services (tests, guidance etc)
  • We have the right to privacy and non-discrimination because of our sexual affiliations (male/females) or because of the way we express ourselves and our way of life.
  • Why are Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights Important to AGYW?
  • Girls and young women, in particular, are denied the ability to exercise these rights. Fulfilling the rights of all children, adolescents and young people is fundamental to achieving gender equality.. All children, adolescents and young people have the right to make their own free and informed choices to have control over their sexual and reproductive health and lives, free from coercion, violence, discrimination and abuse.

Part of the reproductive system and their function

  • The female reproductive system
  • Ovaries: Produce eggs (ova) and hormones such as estrogen and progesterone.
  • Fallopian Tubes: Transport eggs from the ovaries to the uterus. Fertilization typically occurs here.
  • Uterus: Nurture and house a fertilized egg during pregnancy. It also sheds its lining during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur.
  • Endometrium: The lining of the uterus that thickens during the menstrual cycle to prepare for potential implantation of a fertilized egg.
  • Cervix: The lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It allows menstrual blood to flow out and sperm to enter the uterus.
  • Vagina: Serves as the canal for menstrual flow, receives the penis during intercourse, and is the birth canal during delivery.
  • Vulva: The external part of the female genitalia, including the labia, clitoris, and vaginal opening. It protects the internal reproductive organs.
  • Clitoris: Contains erectile tissue and is a primary source of female sexual pleasure.
  • Male Reproductive System
  • Testes: Produce sperm and testosterone.
  • Epididymis: Stores and matures sperm from the testes.
  • Vas Deferens: Transports mature sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
  • Seminal Vesicles: Produce a significant portion of the semen, which provides nutrients for the sperm.
  • Prostate Gland: Adds a fluid to the semen that helps nourish the sperm and enhances sperm motility.
  • Urethra: Carries urine from the bladder and semen from the reproductive system to the outside of the body.
  • Penis: Delivers sperm to the female reproductive tract and serves as the organ for urination.

What is Puberty

Puberty is the time when kids grow into young adults through physical and emotional changes. This doesn’t happen all at once, but slowly over time. It's good to know about the changes that come along with puberty so you know what to expect.

When Does Puberty Start?

Most females will start puberty when they’re 8 to 13 years old, and most males will start between 9 and 14. But it can also be normal to start earlier or later.

How Does Puberty Start?

Hormones from the brain trigger the start of puberty. Hormones are chemical messengers that tell the body what to do. Other puberty hormones come from the adrenal glands, a pair of glands that sit at the top of the kidneys. These hormones lead to the growth of pubic and underarm hair, body odor, and acne.

In : The hormones tell the testicles to make the hormone testosterone and sperm.

In : The hormones tell the ovaries to make the hormone estrogen and triggers the growth and release of eggs.

What Physical Changes Happen During Puberty?

The physical changes that happen during puberty are different for males and females.

Males:

For a male, the physical changes of puberty usually start with the testicles getting bigger. Dark, coarse, curly hair will sprout just above the penis and on the scrotum. The penis and testes will get larger, and  happen more often. Ejaculation — the release of sperm-containing semen —also happens. Ejaculation during sleep is called a “” or nocturnal emission.

Later, hair will grow under the arms and in the beard area. And that first crack in the voice is a sign that the  and will get deeper. Some males get some breast growth (called gynecomastia). It usually goes away in 6 to 18 months. Their body shape begins to change as their shoulders broaden and they gain weight and muscle. A growth spurt usually happens between ages 12 and 15. By age 16, most males have stopped growing, but their muscles will continue to develop.

Females:

For most females, the first physical change of puberty is breast development. It starts with small, firm, tender lumps (called buds) under one or both nipples. The breasts will get larger over the next year or two. Dark, coarse, curly hair will appear on the labia (the folds of skin surrounding the vagina). Later, more hair will grow in the pubic area and under the arms. Their body shape begins to change as their hips widen and they gain weight and body fat. Expect the first period () about 2 years after breast buds appear, usually between the ages of 9 and 16. Most females have a growth spurt about 1–2 years before their period starts. After they get their period, most females grow about 1–2 more inches before growth stops.

What Emotional Changes Happen During Puberty?

Just as those hormones change the way your body looks on the outside, they also change how you feel on the inside. While your body is adjusting to all the new hormones, so is your mind. During puberty, you might feel confused or have  that you've never had before. You may feel anxious about how your  looks. You might feel get upset or lose your temper more than usual, you will experience mood swings, you may start seeking independence which may result to frequent arguments and rebellious behavior.

What Else Should you Know?

Even though everyone goes through puberty, we all go through it a little differently. Some of your friends might have gotten curves, but you haven't yet. Maybe your best friend's voice has changed, and you think you still sound like a kid. But eventually everyone catches up, and the differences will even out.

Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to look. We are all unique, on the inside and the outside. A period is a release of blood from a girl's , out through her vagina. It is a sign that she is getting close to the end of . There is a lot to learn about periods. Here are some common questions that you may have on your mind.

What is menstruation

Menstruation can be defined as the monthly flow of blood from the uterus through the vagina. It begins from the age of 9-12 years. The first menstruation in girls is called menarche and the end of menstruation in women is known as menopause and normally from 45 years and above

When Do Most Girls Get Their Period?

Most girls get their first period when they're around 12. But getting it any time between age 10 and 15 is OK. Every girl's body has its own schedule. There isn't one right age for a girl to get her period. But there are some clues that it will start soon:

Most of the time, a girl gets her period about 2 years after her breasts start to develop.

Another sign is  fluid (sort of like mucus) that a girl might see or feel on her underwear. This discharge usually begins about 6 months to a year before a girl gets her first period.

What Causes a Period?

A period happens because of changes in  in the body. Hormones are chemical messengers. The ovaries release the female hormones  and . These hormones cause the lining of the uterus (or womb) to build up. The built-up lining is ready for a fertilized egg to attach to and start developing. If there is no fertilized egg, the lining breaks down and bleeds. Then the same process happens all over again. It usually takes about a month for the lining to build up, then break down. That is why most girls and women get their periods around once a month.

How Does Ovulation Relate to Periods?

Ovulation is the release of an egg from the ovaries. The same hormones that cause the uterus lining to build up also cause an egg to leave one of the ovaries. The egg travels through a thin tube called a fallopian tube to the uterus. If the egg is fertilized by a sperm cell, it attaches to the wall of the uterus, where over time it develops into a baby. If the egg is not fertilized, the uterus lining breaks down and bleeds, causing a period.

How does a girl feel when period is about to begin and during her period?

When her period begins, the levels of the hormones estrogen and progesterone are low; thus causing some discomfort as follows:

Breasts are changing

-Irritation

-Menstrual cramps (lemon???)

-Feeling tired

-Constipation or have diarrhea (Drink a lot of water)

-Bloated and gassy (eat more fruits and vegetables)

-Headache

-Mood swings etc.. (cheer up

Do Periods Happen Regularly When Menstruation Starts?

For the first few years after a girl starts her period, it may not come regularly. This is normal at first. By about 2–3 years after her first period, a girl's periods should be coming around once every 4–5 weeks.

Can a Girl Get Pregnant as Soon as Her Period Starts?

Yes! a girl can get pregnant as soon as her period starts. A girl can even get pregnant right before her very first period. This is because a girl's hormones might already be active. The hormones may have led to  and the building of the uterine wall. If a girl has sex, she can get pregnant, even though she has never had a period.

How Long Do Periods Last?

Periods usually last about 5 days. But a period can be shorter or last longer.

How Often Does a Period Happen?

Periods usually happen about once every 4–5 weeks. But some girls get their periods a little less or more often.

What should I do when I start Menstruating?

You have  about how to deal with period blood. You may need to experiment a bit to find which works best for you. Some girls use only one method and others switch between different methods.

Most girls use pads when they first get their period. Pads are made of cotton and come in lots of different sizes and shapes. They have sticky strips that attach to the underwear.

Many girls find tampons more convenient than pads, especially when playing sports or swimming. A tampon is a cotton plug that a girl puts into her vagina. Most tampons come with an applicator that guides the tampon into place. The tampon absorbs the blood. Don't leave a tampon in for more than 8 hours because this can increase your risk of a serious infection called .

Some girls prefer a menstrual cup. Most menstrual cups are made of silicone. To use a menstrual cup, a girl inserts it into her vagina. It holds the blood until she empties it.

If you cannot afford any of the above mentioned, you can get any clean cotton cloth (towel, wrapper or dress) cut into about 3 millimeters long, neatly fold and wear on your panties. Make sure to change it anytime you feel wet. Wash them in hot water with soap, and dry under the sun before the next wear.

Menstrual kit before and during your period:

  • Menstrual Product eg pads, tampons, menstrual cups etc
  • Wipes or a small hand sanitizer
  • A couple of pairs of comfortable, easily washable underwear.
  • A pair of comfortable pants or leggings and a top, just in case you need a fresh change.
  • A bottle of water
  • Hygiene Creams or Spray
  • Discreet bags for used products if you're on the go and don’t have access to a trash bin.
  • Pain Management Tools eg warm bath, if indicated

How Much Blood Comes Out during Menstruation?

It may look like a lot of blood, but a girl usually only loses a few tablespoons of blood during the whole period. Most girls need to change their pad, tampon, or menstrual cup about 3‒6 times a day.

Will I Have Periods for the Rest of My Life?

When women reach menopause (around age 45‒55), their periods will permanently stop. Women also won't have a period while they are .

What is PMS?

PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is when a girl has emotional and physical symptoms that happen before or during her period. These symptoms can include moodiness, sadness, anxiety, bloating, and acne. The symptoms go away after the first few days of a period.

What Can I Do About Cramps?

Many girls have cramps with their period, especially in the first few days. If cramps bother you, you can try:

a warm heating pad on your belly

taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin, or store brand) or naproxen (Aleve or store brand)

Should I Watch out for any Problems?

Most girls don't have any problems with their periods. Talk to an adult or see a doctor if you:

are 15 and haven't started your period

have had your period for more than 2 years and it still doesn't come regularly (about every 4–5 weeks)

Cramps are severe, and you seem to be bleeding between periods

have severe cramps that don't get better with ibuprofen or naproxen 

have very heavy bleeding (bleeding that goes through a pad or tampon faster than every 1 hour)

have periods that last more than about a week

It has been 3 months since your last period

have severe PMS that gets in the way of your everyday activities

Daily Checklist for a Changing body

  • Shower preferably twice a day or at least once a day
  • Clean vagina ONLY with fresh water, NO douching liquids or chemicals.
  • Use deodorant or anti- per spirant on the underarms
  • Wash face daily to help prevent acne
  • Brush teeth twice per day
  • Eat well balanced diets
  • Get plenty of exercise and rest
  • Do not wear under garments repeatedly, it is preferable to wash and dry them under the sun before wearing again.

2.4.1. HIV

What is HIV

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is a virus that attacks cells that help the body fight infects. NB. There is no cure but it is treatable with medicine

H -uman

Found only in humans

Transmitted among humans

Preventable by humans

I -mmunodefiency

Body lacks ability to fight off infections

V -irus

Type of germ

Lives and reproduces in body cells

HIV is a virus that damages the immune system

-The immune system helps the body fight off infections

-AIDS is a disease that can develop in people with HIV

-It’s the most advanced stage of HIV

-But just because a person has HIV doesn’t mean they’ll develop AIDS

-HIV kills CD4 cells

-Healthy adults generally have a CD4 count of per cubic millimeter

-. A person with HIV whose CD4 count falls below per cubic millimeter will be diagnosed with AIDS

What is the Connection between HIV and AIDS

To develop AIDS, a person has to have contracted HIV. But having HIV doesn’t necessarily mean that someone will develop AIDS.

Cases of HIV progress through three stages:

stage 1: , the first few weeks after transmission

stage 2: clinical latency, or chronic stage

stage 3: AIDS

As HIV lowers the CD4 cell count, the immune system weakens. A typical adult’s CD4 count is 500 to 1,500 per cubic millimeter. A person with a count below 200 is considered to have AIDS.

Myths about HIV and AIDS. Don’t be fooled Get the facts. The below table show some myths and right facts.

MYTHS AND RIGHT FACTS

HIV TRANSMISSION

  • HIV can be transmitted from one person to another through blood, semen, vaginal fluid, rectal fluid, and breast milk. This can happen during:
  • Blood
  • semen
  • Vaginal and rectal fluids
  • breastmilk

Some of the ways HIV is spread from person to person include:

through vaginal or anal sex , especially among men who have sex with men

by sharing needles, syringes, and other items for injection drug use

by sharing tattoo equipment without sterilizing it between uses

during pregnancy, labor, or delivery from a woman to her baby

during breastfeeding

through “pre-mastication,” or chewing a baby’s food before feeding it to them

through exposure to the blood of someone living with HIV, such as through a needle stick

through a blood transfusion or organ and tissue transplant.

More ways HIV/AIDS can be Passed on (but rarely)

oral sex (only if there are bleeding gums or open sores in the person’s mouth)

-being bitten by a person with HIV (only if the saliva is bloody or there are open sores in the person’s mouth)

-contact between broken skin, wounds, or mucous membranes and the blood of someone living with HIV

HIV/AIDS cannot be Passed on

  • skin-to-skin contact
  • hugging, shaking hands, or kissing
  • air or water
  • sharing food or drinks, including drinking fountains
  • saliva, tears, or sweat (unless mixed with the blood of a person with HIV)
  • sharing a toilet, towels, or bedding
  • mosquitoes or other insects

You CANNOT get HIV from…

Tears

Saliva

Sweat

Urine of an HIV infected person

What is window Period for HIV

It is the time between first infection of HIV and when the test can reliably detect the HIV infection.

  • When a person gets infected it may take 6 weeks or up to 3 months before antibodies to HIV are detected in the blood
  • The HIV test looks for antibodies. When these antibodies are detected the person is diagnosed HIV positive
  • A person can be positive and the test shows negative because the test was done during the window period

Early Signs & Symptoms of HIV

Early symptoms of HIV can include:

- fever

- chills

- swollen lymph nodes

- general aches and pains

- skin rash

- sore throat

- headache

- nausea

- upset stomach

- diarrhea

Remember these are symptoms of many other illnesses.

Why HIV Rates are NOT Going Down especially for AGYW

Sex at an early age

Little life-skills and sex education

Little condom use

Multiple partners

Stigma and Discrimination

Sex for money or sex for other things

Substance abuse: Ganja, cocaine, alcohol

Gender inequity and gender roles

STI and HIV – The Link

Persons with a history of STIs are more likely to get HIV because:

Persons with STIs are more likely to have sores and small breaks in the skin and lining of their genitals. HIV can more easily enter the body through these breaks.

HIV PREVENTION

Talk with partner about HIV

Use a condom with your regular and non-regular clients, and partners every time you have sex

Reduce the number of main partners

Get tested. Know your status

Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP). If you don't have HIV you can protect yourself by taking anti-HIV medication called oral PrEP

Post Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP). If you’ve been exposed to HIV you can prevent infection by taking HIV medication - PEP within 72 hours of exposure.

Antiretroviral Therapy (ART). If you’re HIV positive you can prevent transmission to others by taking HIV medication

Additional methods you can use to reduce the risk of HIV transmission during sex are:

  • Using male or female condoms every time you have sex - including vaginal, anal and oral sex
  • Using water-based or silicone-based lubricant to prevent condoms from breaking and dry sex.
  • Regularly testing for STIs and treating them immediately.
  • Abstaining, reducing your number of sexual partners and knowing you partner’s status.

Mothers with HIV can reduce the risk of HIV transmission to their baby by:

  • Taking HIV medication during pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding.
  • Treating their baby with HIV medication.
  • HIV-positive people who do not wish to become pregnant can use family planning to prevent unintended pregnancy.
  • If you are HIV positive and thinking of having a baby, talk to a doctor about the best way to reduce the risk of transmission

You can reduce the risk of HIV transmission through blood by:

  • Avoiding contact with other people’s blood.
  • Never using a needle that has been used by someone else

AGAIN and AGAIN! You cannot get HIV from touching, kissing or sharing food and drink with someone who is HIV positive

ADDITIONAL SYMPTOMS ESPECIALLY IN WOMEN

In addition, women with HIV are at increased risk of:

  • recurrent
  • other vaginal infections, including bacterial vaginosis
  • pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
  • menstrual cycle changes
  • , which can cause and lead to

CARE RESPONSE

  • Create a safe space
  • A safe space is both physically and emotionally safe. Make sure you’re somewhere private, where they feel physically safe. Explain that you’re just there to listen – you won’t judge them or tell them what to do. Let them know they can trust you to protect their confidentiality.
  • Actively Listen
  • Show them you’re listening deeply and with empathy. Use your body language to communicate that you’re paying attention. Give them space to talk, and acknowledge and validate their feelings.
  • Reassure
  • Reassure them by letting them know they’re not alone, you’re there for them and their feelings are valid. If they’ve shared an experience of violence, let them know that you believe them and it’s not their fault.
  • Empower and Support
  • Let them know they are in control of what happens next. Help them to identify their needs and consider their options. Be ready to provide them with information about support services they can access.

Test and Prevent

  • Everybody has a responsibility to contribute to the prevention of HIV in our community!

Other ways people living with HIV can improve their health include:

Steps to help people living with HIV feel their best include:

  • fueling their body with a well-balanced diet
  • exercising regularly
  • getting plenty of rest
  • avoiding tobacco and other drugs
  • reporting any new symptoms to their healthcare ----provider right away

2.4.2. SEXUALLY TRANSMISSIBLE INFECTIONS (STIs)

An infection transmitted through sexual contact, caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites.

More than 30 different bacteria, viruses and parasites are transmitted through sexual contact.

STIs are spread predominantly by sexual contact, including vaginal, anal and oral sex. Some STIs can also be spread through non-sexual means such as via blood or blood products. Many STIs—including syphilis, hepatitis B, HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, herpes, and HPV—can also be transmitted from mother to child during pregnancy and childbirth.

A person can have an STI without having obvious symptoms of disease. Common symptoms of STIs include vaginal discharge, urethral discharge or burning in men, genital ulcers, and abdominal pain.

Eight of these infections are linked to the greatest incidence of sexually transmitted disease.

4 Common types of STI - curable

  • Syphilis: A bacterial infection usually spread by sexual contact that starts as a painless sore.
  • Chlamydia: A common, sexually transmitted infection that may not cause symptoms.
  • Gonorrhea: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that, if untreated, may cause infertility.
  • Trichomoniasis: a common sexually transmitted infection caused by a parasite. In women, it can cause a foul-smelling vaginal discharge, genital itching and painful urination. Men who have it typically have no symptoms.

4 common types can’t be cured

  • Hepatitis B:a vaccine-preventable liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). spread when blood, semen, or other body fluids from a person infected with the virus enters the body of someone who is not infected.
  • Herpes simplex virus (HSV or herpes): A common sexually transmitted infection marked by genital pain and sores.
  • HIV: HIV causes AIDS and interferes with the body's ability to fight infections
  • Human papillomavirus (HPV): An infection that causes warts in various parts of the body, depending on the strain

Treatment of STIs

  • Effective treatment is currently available for several STIs.
  • Three bacterial STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis) and one parasitic STI (trichomoniasis) are generally curable with existing, effective single-dose regimens of antibiotics.
  • For herpes and HIV, the most effective medications available are antivirals that can modulate the course of the disease, though they cannot cure the disease.
  • For hepatitis B, antiviral medications can help to fight the virus and slow damage to the liver.
  • To interrupt transmission of infection and prevent re-infection, treating sexual partners is an important component of STI case management.

SCOPE OF THE PROBLEM

STIs have a profound impact on sexual and reproductive health worldwide.

  • STIs like herpes and syphilis can increase the risk of HIV acquisition three-fold or more.
  • Mother-to-child transmission of STIs can result in stillbirth, neonatal death, low-birth-weight and prematurity, sepsis, pneumonia, neonatal conjunctivitis, and congenital deformities. Approximately 1 million pregnant women were estimated to have active syphilis in 2016, resulting in over 350 000 adverse birth outcomes of which 200 000 occurred as stillbirth or neonatal death (5).
  • HPV infection causes 570 000 cases of cervical cancer and over 300 000 cervical cancer deaths each year (6).
  • STIs such as gonorrhoea and chlamydia are major causes of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and infertility in women.

Prevention of STIs

Counselling and behavioural approaches

Offer primary prevention against STIs (including HIV), as well as against unintended pregnancies. These include:

comprehensive sexuality education,

STI and HIV pre- and post-test counselling;

safer sex/risk-reduction counselling, condom promotion;

STI interventions targeted to key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men and people who inject drugs; and

STI prevention education and counselling tailored to the needs of adolescents.

In addition, counselling can improve people’s ability to recognize the symptoms of STIs and increase the likelihood they will seek care or encourage a sexual partner to do so. Unfortunately, lack of public awareness, lack of training of health workers, and long-standing, widespread stigma around STIs remain barriers to greater and more effective use of these interventions.

Barrier methods

When used correctly and consistently, condoms offer one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs, including HIV. Female condoms are effective and safe, but are not used as widely by national programmes as male condoms.

2.5. Contraception

Comprehensive Sexual Health Education suggests abstinence as the preferred sexual behavior amongst teens. Abstaining from sexual activity that involves exchange of bodily fluids and/or genital to genital or skin to genital contact is the only sure way of avoiding the risk of pregnancy or sexually transmitted infections. Postponement of initial sexual activity, adherence to one sexual partner and protected sexual intercourse are sequentially offered as the next best alternatives.

MYTHSRIGHT FACTS
You can tell someone has HIV just by looking at themThere is no way to tell if someone has HIV by looking at them. Many people have HIV without knowing it. The only way to know if you are HIV positive is to have your blood tested.
You should avoid people who have HIV in case they give it to you.You cannot catch HIV like you catch the flu. HIV can only be transmitted when body fluid—either blood, semen, vaginal fluid, rectal fluid, or breast milk—enters the bloodstream of an HIV-negative person. You cannot get HIV through kissing, hugging, using the same utensils, using the same toilet, mosquitoes or any other casual contact.
Using condoms or oral PrEP means you don’t trust your partner.Protecting yourself from HIV is not about trust. Anyone can be HIV positive, and many people don’t know their status. If you are in a loving and trusting relationship, you should both want to protect each other from HIV. This means having safer sex, getting tested regularly and considering oral PrEP
Adolescent girls and young women, gay men and other men who have sex with men, sex workers and transgender people are more at risk of HIV because they are promiscuous.Actually, there are many biological reasons that these groups are vulnerable to HIV. It’s easier for HIV to enter through the walls of the vagina than it is through the penis, and unprotected receptive anal sex makes people the most vulnerable to HIV. It’s also harder for these groups to protect themselves from HIV because society doesn’t treat them equally, and they have less power in their relationships to negotiate safer sex. Oral PrEP can help people take control of their health!
Some herbs can protect you from HIV when you put them in your vagina.here are no herbs or natural remedies that can prevent or cure HIV. Inserting plants or herbs into your vagina can increase your risk of HIV; it can dry out the vagina, which can lead to tears and allow HIV to enter the body more easily.
If I use lubricant, I’m protected against HIV.Using water-based or silicone-based lubricant can reduce HIV vulnerability by keeping condoms from breaking or slipping, but using lubricant alone does not provide much HIV protection.
HIV-positive women should not breastfeed their babies.It’s not that simple. Breastfeeding provides many nutrients and protective factors to a baby, and HIV transmission can be prevented with the right medication. HIV-positive mothers should work with their doctor to find the best option.
If you get HIV you will get sick and die.While there is no cure for HIV, there are treatments available, known as antiretrovirals, or ARVs for short. If treatment is started early and taken consistently, a person with HIV can live a long and healthy life without ever developing AIDS. These medications can also help prevent transmission to others
TestPreventRespondtreat
Test for HIV and STIs – and do it regularly Most HIV transmissions come from people who don’t know they’re HIV positive. Knowing you’re HIV positive gives you the power to protect your health and prevent transmission to others. Knowing your partner’s status is also important for making decisions about HIV preventionProtect yourself from HIV transmission every time you have sex. Use male condoms and female condoms. Male and female condoms put a barrier between the most delicate skin and body fluids that may contain HIV and other STIs. Using lubricant (water- or silicone-based) will help prevent condoms from breaking. Prevent Oral PrEP (preexposure prophylaxis) Oral PrEP is a medication that an HIVnegative person can take to protect themselves from HIV. It creates a shield around a person’s blood cells to protect them from HIV. When a person takes oral PrEP every day and they’re exposed to HIV, it can’t infect their blood cells. The virus will die, and the person won’t get HIV. Oral PrEP doesn’t protect you against STIs, so it’s best to always use a condom Abstinence, reducing your number of sexual partners, can also help prevent HIVIf you’ve been exposed to HIV, act quickly! If you’re worried you might have been exposed to HIV, you can take emergency medication to reduce the risk that you’ll get HIV Respond quickly PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) If HIV makes it into the body, PEP can stop it from spreading to other cells. When HIV can’t spread, it dies. This may prevent a person from becoming HIV positive. PEP must be started within 72 hours of exposure and taken every day for 4 weeksIf you’ve been diagnosed with HIV, start treatment as soon as possible to stay healthy and prevent transmission. If you find out you have HIV, it’s important to start treatment right away. It won’t cure HIV, but it can stop the virus from spreading and developing into AIDS – meaning that you can live a long and healthy life. HIV treatment also reduces the risk that you’ll transmit HIV to others. Treatment ART (Antiretroviral therapy) ART is a combination of medications that work together to reduce the amount of HIV in a person’s body and boost their immune system. If treatment is started early and taken every day, the amount of HIV in a person’s blood can become so low that there’s not enough of the virus to pass on to others. This is called an undetectable viral load.

What is contraception?

Contraception occurs by either preventing the fertilization of an ovum (egg) by the sperm cell, or the prevention of implantation of the embryo (fertilized egg) into the lining of the uterus.

Why is it important to learn about contraception?

Teaching birth control/contraception is not an assumption that you are sexually active, but it is a factual information which is critical to make healthy decisions now and in the future.

Types of contraception methods include:

Abstinence

Condoms

The Fertility awareness or calendar use.

  • Emergency Contraception/Plan B (the “morning after pill”)
  • Hormonal pills: A pill is taken orally each day 
  • Birth control patch: This is a patch that sticks to the skin, delivers hormones through the skin, and is changed once per week for three weeks
  • Vaginal ring: This is a small flexible device that is inserted into the vagina once a month for three weeks

Depo-Provera shot: This is an injection into the muscle every 12 weeks 

Hormone-releasing intrauterine device (IUD): This is a tiny, T-shaped device that is inserted into the uterus and can stay in place for three to six years depending on the IUD that is chosen

Birth control implant: This is a small, thin rod that is inserted under the skin of the arm for 3 to 5 years (one in 10 women stopped using this method because of unfavorable bleeding changes)

Dual use

It should be noted that amongst all the contraceptive methods listed above, ABSTINENCE remains the most reliable method with 100% guarantee to prevent unwanted pregnancies.

Barriers to contraceptive adoption and sustained use

i) Limited method choice and access

Contraceptive use depends on a person’s knowledge of methods and sources of supplies. There is also usually a correlation between travel time from a woman’s home to any health clinic and the likelihood that she will use a contraceptive

ii) Financial costs

The prices of contraceptives vary widely in different markets and between branded and generic products. The financial cost of contraceptives may influence choice of method and adoption.

iii) Women’s status and perceptions of partner’s views

The social construction of gender and women’s position within society affects many aspects of family planning. Fertility preferences can be derived from the social and economic status gained by conforming to cultural expectations about motherhood rather than through personal choice, for example by having large families, sons or proving fertility by having children straight after marriage. Again women are often financially dependent on men and may lack access to cash to purchase contraceptives and may also be coerced into making reproductive choices based on the wishes of others.

iv) Medical and legal restrictions

Practices, derived at least partly from a medical rationale, which result in a scientifically unjustifiable impediment to, or denial of, contraception. For example, women being subjected to unnecessary medical procedures as a prerequisite for gaining access to contraceptive methods may act as a barrier. Even where family planning services are physically accessible and economic barriers to access are few, medical barriers to contraceptive services— such as overspecialisation, demanding husbands’ consent, eligibility restrictions and process hurdles—can limit women’s use of services

v) Provider bias

Service providers sometimes deny access to a family planning method as a result of their own prejudices about the method or its delivery system or the status of the person asking for family planning

vi) Misinformation

Side effects, lack of accurate information, and misinformation commonly interact to create a disproportionate fear of fertility regulation methods. For instance, young people fear using either the pill or injectable contraceptives because they believed that these methods would make them permanently sterile.

2.6. Pregnancy

Pregnancy is a period in which a fetus develops inside a woman's womb or uterus. It can also be defined as the condition of carrying a developing embryo or fetus within the female body. It typically lasts about 40 weeks, measured from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP)

Signs of pregnancy

  • Missed Period
  • Nausea and Vomiting
  • Tender Breast
  • Fatigue
  • Frequent Urination.
  • Mood Swings.
  • Food Cravings
  • Increased Sensitivity to Smell
  • Headaches or Dizziness.

If you suspect you might be pregnant, taking a home pregnancy test or visiting a healthcare provider can give you a definitive answer.

Unintended Pregnancy. What is it?

An unintended pregnancy is a pregnancy that is either occurring earlier than desired or unwanted occurring when no children are desired. Statistically it is estimated Approximately 44% of pregnancies worldwide are unintended and about 61% of unintended pregnancies end in abortion, 24% result in an unplanned birth, and 15% in miscarriage.

Causes of unintended pregnancy

Lack of Comprehensive Sexual Education leading to uninformed decisions.

Sexual Violence Pregnancies resulting from rape or coerced sex.

Ineffectiveness of contraceptive methods due to incorrect use or failure of the method itself.

Lack of Access to Contraception. Barriers to obtaining and using contraceptives, including cost, availability, and lack of information.

Societal norms and expectations influencing contraceptive use and sexual behavior.

Peer pressure the leads into reckless behaviors.

Having multiply sexual partners

Consequences of unintended pregnancy for girls

Higher risk of maternal morbidity and mortality, especially in cases of unsafe abortion.

Increased financial strain on families and healthcare systems.

Emotional stress, anxiety, and depression for the individual and parents.

Potential stigma and social repercussions, particularly for unmarried women and girls.

Children from unintended pregnancies may face adverse health and developmental outcomes due to potential lack of preparation and resources.

Unintended pregnancies can interrupt or end educational and career aspirations, particularly for young women.

Consequences of unintended pregnancy for boys

Emotional stress, anxiety and depression for the individual and parents.

School drop out

Increased financial strain on families and healthcare systems.

Unintended parenting

How Can Unintended Pregnancy Be Prevented

Providing accurate, age-appropriate information about sexual and reproductive health, including contraception, consent, and healthy relationships.

Right use and access to contraception

Improving access to quality reproductive health services and counselling

Promoting gender equality and empowering women and girls to make informed decisions about their reproductive health.

Support for Victims of Sexual Violence including access to emergency contraception, for survivors.

Myths about pregnancy prevention

  • Douching with various solutions after sexual intercourse, which does not kill all sperm.
  • Drinking vast amounts of medication or alcohol which, does nothing to prevent pregnancy and could cause harm.
  • Withdrawal before orgasm (pulling out), which does not ensure sperm are not released into the vaginal area because pre-ejaculate can be unknowingly released.
  • Using Saran Wrap, instead of a condom which, does not protect against pregnancy.

Ways to express friendship and love to another person.

  • Express Appreciation Regularly tell the people what you appreciate about them and how much they mean to you.
  • Make an effort to spend time with the people, whether through activities you both enjoy or simply being present.
  • Perform small acts of kindness, such as running an errand for them, helping with a task, or bringing them their favorite treat.
  • Surprise them with something they like or need, such as a book by their favorite author or a favorite snack.
  • Simply being there for someone during challenging times can provide comfort and show you care.
  • Offer encouragement and support for their goals, dreams, and endeavors. Celebrate their achievements and offer a helping hand when needed.
  • Engage in activities that both of you enjoy, such as going to a concert, hiking, or cooking a meal together. Shared experiences can strengthen bonds.
  • Honor their personal space and boundaries. Respect their preferences and individuality.

(Friendship, Love, Romantic relationship and Dating)

Relationships are avenues where adolescents can safely feel and express respect for themselves and others.  .  .  . Types of relationships include;

Friendship: Friendships are an essential part of adolescent development. . . .

Love: Love is a strong feeling of warm personal attachment or deep affection for someone, such as for a parent, child or friend. Love is considered to be positive, with its  representing human , , and —"the unselfish, loyal and benevolent concern for the good of another". Most adolescents misinterpret love as sex, but LOVE IS NOT SEX, neither is sex a component of love.

Romantic relationship: Romantic relationships are often reserved for much matured adults because it is linked in a way adults. It comes along with all the other changes going on during this period - physical, social, and emotional. Adolescents can spend a lot of time thinking about romantic relationships, and this type of relationship can bring many emotional ups and downs for them, which could be very complicated to handle by so doing taking a negative toll on their lives, and distracting them from their education which should be their main focus.

Dating: Otherwise known as courtship, dating is a higher stage of a romantic relationship in which two individuals engage in activities together, most often with the intention of evaluating each other's suitability as a partner in a future  such as marriage. It usually consist of  carried out by the couple either alone or with others.

Infatuation; Refers to an intense but often short-lived passion or admiration for someone, usually characterized by strong feelings of attraction and idealization. Infatuation can involve obsessive thoughts and a heightened focus on the person's physical or superficial traits, often lacking the depth and stability found in more enduring emotional connections.

Sexual Attraction; is a desire for physical intimacy with someone based primarily on sexual desire. It is focused on the physical and sexual aspects of the person rather than emotional or romantic connection. Sexual attraction can exist independently of emotional involvement or a deeper relationship.

Love vs. Infatuation: Love is more enduring and deeper, involving emotional commitment and mutual understanding, while infatuation is often intense but fleeting, focused on surface-level qualities and often idealized.

Friendship vs. Romantic Love: Friendship is based on mutual support and respect, while romantic love involves a deeper emotional connection, often including physical intimacy and long-term commitment.

Sexual Attraction vs. Emotional Connection: Sexual attraction is primarily about physical desire and can exist without emotional intimacy, whereas emotional connection involves deeper feelings of affection and understanding that go beyond physical attraction.

  • Respect each other: Respect is the foundation of any healthy relationship. .
  • Build trust: Trust is essential in any healthy relationship. .

Characteristics of Unhealthy Relationships

Unhealthy relationships can have a significant detrimental impact on your health, happiness, and overall well-being. . Here are some common characteristics of unhealthy relationships:

Control: One person may try to control the other person’s life through intimidation, manipulation, or other means. .

Lack of trust: Unhealthy relationships are often marked by a lack of trust. .

Poor communication: Communication is key in any healthy relationship. .

Consistent negativity: In unhealthy relationships, there may be a consistent negative tone or atmosphere. .

Manipulation: One person may try to manipulate the other person into doing what they want. .

.

or better still cut off from such a relationship. Remember that everyone deserves to be in a healthy and safe relationship.

Ways in managing sexual emotions as a young person

  • Reflect on your sexual emotions and desires to understand what triggers them and how they affect you. Recognize whether these feelings are tied to a specific person, situation, or general emotions.
  • Clarify your personal values and boundaries regarding sex. Understanding what you want and don’t want can help you make informed decisions and manage your emotions more effectively.
  • If you’re in a relationship, communicate openly and honestly with your partner about your sexual needs, desires, and boundaries. Effective communication can prevent misunderstandings and ensure that both partners feel respected and understood. Respecting the other person’s boundaries
  • Find healthy ways to channel sexual emotions. Engaging in hobbies, exercise, or creative activities can provide an outlet for intense emotions and reduce the focus on sexual desire.
  • Learn about human sexuality, including the emotional and physical aspects. Understanding sexual health and emotions can help you manage them more effectively and make informed choices.
  • If sexual emotions become overwhelming or difficult to manage, consider seeking guidance from a therapist or counselor specializing in sexual health.
  • Building Healthy Relationships can provide a stable foundation for managing sexual emotions.
  • Be mindful of any compulsive behaviors related to sexual activity, such as excessive pornography consumption or impulsive decisions

2.1. KEY DEFINITIONS

What is Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH)

What is Sexual Health

Sexual health is an integral part of overall health, well-being and quality of life. It is a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality, and not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity.

Sexual health requires a positive and respectful approach to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the possibility of having pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free of coercion, discrimination and violence. For sexual health to be attained and maintained, the sexual rights of all people must be respected, protected and fulfilled.

What is Reproductive Health

Reproductive health (RH) implies that people are able to have a responsible, satisfying and safe sex life and that they have the capability to have children and the freedom to decide if, when and how often to do so.

Linking Sexual and Reproductive Health to Rights

  • What are the Rights
  • The right to health care
  • The right to privacy
  • The right to participation
  • The right to protection
  • The right to non-discrimination
  • The right to obtain information
  • The right to express opinion
  • The right learning (and education)
  • The right to life and growth to the fullest possible extent

.

Description of linkage

  • Enjoyment of SRH is a basic part of the right to enjoy life and health and grow to the fullest possible extent
  • We have the right to protection from sexual abuse, STIs, early marriage, unsafe abortion and undesired pregnancy
  • We have the right to express opinion and feelings of sexuality and we have the right to participation in decisions that concerns us
  • We have the right to knowledge/education/sex education and the right to obtain SRH services (tests, guidance etc)
  • We have the right to privacy and non-discrimination because of our sexual affiliations (male/females) or because of the way we express ourselves and our way of life.
  • Why are Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights Important to AGYW?
  • Girls and young women, in particular, are denied the ability to exercise these rights. Fulfilling the rights of all children, adolescents and young people is fundamental to achieving gender equality.. All children, adolescents and young people have the right to make their own free and informed choices to have control over their sexual and reproductive health and lives, free from coercion, violence, discrimination and abuse.

Part of the reproductive system and their function

  • The female reproductive system
  • Ovaries: Produce eggs (ova) and hormones such as estrogen and progesterone.
  • Fallopian Tubes: Transport eggs from the ovaries to the uterus. Fertilization typically occurs here.
  • Uterus: Nurture and house a fertilized egg during pregnancy. It also sheds its lining during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur.
  • Endometrium: The lining of the uterus that thickens during the menstrual cycle to prepare for potential implantation of a fertilized egg.
  • Cervix: The lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It allows menstrual blood to flow out and sperm to enter the uterus.
  • Vagina: Serves as the canal for menstrual flow, receives the penis during intercourse, and is the birth canal during delivery.
  • Vulva: The external part of the female genitalia, including the labia, clitoris, and vaginal opening. It protects the internal reproductive organs.
  • Clitoris: Contains erectile tissue and is a primary source of female sexual pleasure.
  • Male Reproductive System
  • Testes: Produce sperm and testosterone.
  • Epididymis: Stores and matures sperm from the testes.
  • Vas Deferens: Transports mature sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
  • Seminal Vesicles: Produce a significant portion of the semen, which provides nutrients for the sperm.
  • Prostate Gland: Adds a fluid to the semen that helps nourish the sperm and enhances sperm motility.
  • Urethra: Carries urine from the bladder and semen from the reproductive system to the outside of the body.
  • Penis: Delivers sperm to the female reproductive tract and serves as the organ for urination.

• Menstrual Hygiene and Management

What is menstruation

Menstruation can be defined as the monthly flow of blood from the uterus through the vagina. It begins from the age of 9-12 years. The first menstruation in girls is called menarche and the end of menstruation in women is known as menopause and normally from 45 years and above

When Do Most Girls Get Their Period?

Most girls get their first period when they're around 12. But getting it any time between age 10 and 15 is OK. Every girl's body has its own schedule. There isn't one right age for a girl to get her period. But there are some clues that it will start soon:

Most of the time, a girl gets her period about 2 years after her breasts start to develop.

Another sign is  fluid (sort of like mucus) that a girl might see or feel on her underwear. This discharge usually begins about 6 months to a year before a girl gets her first period.

What Causes a Period? A period happens because of changes in  in the body. Hormones are chemical messengers. The ovaries release the female hormones  and . These hormones cause the lining of the uterus (or womb) to build up. The built-up lining is ready for a fertilized egg to attach to and start developing. If there is no fertilized egg, the lining breaks down and bleeds. Then the same process happens all over again. It usually takes about a month for the lining to build up, then break down. That is why most girls and women get their periods around once a month.

How Does Ovulation Relate to Periods?

Ovulation is the release of an egg from the ovaries. The same hormones that cause the uterus lining to build up also cause an egg to leave one of the ovaries. The egg travels through a thin tube called a fallopian tube to the uterus. If the egg is fertilized by a sperm cell, it attaches to the wall of the uterus, where over time it develops into a baby. If the egg is not fertilized, the uterus lining breaks down and bleeds, causing a period.

How does a girl feel when period is about to start or when she is on her period?

When her period begins, the levels of the hormones estrogen and progesterone are low; thus causing some discomfort as follows:-

-Breasts are changing

-Irritation

-Menstrual cramps (lemon???)

-Feeling tired

-Constipation or have diarrhea (Drink a lot of water)

-Bloated and gassy (eat more fruits and vegetables)

-Headache

-Mood swings etc.. (cheer up)

Menstrual kit before and during your period:

  • Menstrual Product eg pads, tampons, menstrual cups etc
  • Wipes or a small hand sanitizer
  • A couple of pairs of comfortable, easily washable underwear.
  • A pair of comfortable pants or leggings and a top, just in case you need a fresh change.
  • A bottle of water
  • Hygiene Creams or Spray
  • Discreet bags for used products if you're on the go and don’t have access to a trash bin.
  • Pain Management Tools eg warm bath, if indicated

Do Periods Happen Regularly When Menstruation Starts?

For the first few years after a girl starts her period, it may not come regularly. This is normal at first. By about 2–3 years after her first period, a girl's periods should be coming around once every 4–5 weeks.

Can a Girl Get Pregnant as Soon as Her Period Starts?

Yes! a girl can get pregnant as soon as her period starts. A girl can even get pregnant right before her very first period. This is because a girl's hormones might already be active. The hormones may have led to  and the building of the uterine wall. If a girl has sex, she can get pregnant, even though she has never had a period.

How Long Do Periods Last?

Periods usually last about 5 days. But a period can be shorter or last longer.

How Often Does a Period Happen?

Periods usually happen about once every 4–5 weeks. But some girls get their periods a little less or more often.

What should I do when I start Menstruating?

You have  about how to deal with period blood. You may need to experiment a bit to find which works best for you. Some girls use only one method and others switch between different methods.

Most girls use pads when they first get their period. Pads are made of cotton and come in lots of different sizes and shapes. They have sticky strips that attach to the underwear.

Many girls find tampons more convenient than pads, especially when playing sports or swimming. A tampon is a cotton plug that a girl puts into her vagina. Most tampons come with an applicator that guides the tampon into place. The tampon absorbs the blood. Don't leave a tampon in for more than 8 hours because this can increase your risk of a serious infection called .

Some girls prefer a menstrual cup. Most menstrual cups are made of silicone. To use a menstrual cup, a girl inserts it into her vagina. It holds the blood until she empties it.

If you cannot afford any of the above mentioned, you can get any clean cotton cloth (towel, wrapper or dress) cut into about 3 millimeters long, neatly fold and wear on your panties. Make sure to change it anytime you feel wet. Wash them in hot water with soap, and dry under the sun before the next wear.

How Much Blood Comes Out during Menstruation?

It may look like a lot of blood, but a girl usually only loses a few tablespoons of blood during the whole period. Most girls need to change their pad, tampon, or menstrual cup about 3‒6 times a day.

Will I Have Periods for the Rest of My Life?

When women reach menopause (around age 45‒55), their periods will permanently stop. Women also won't have a period while they are .

What is PMS?

PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is when a girl has emotional and physical symptoms that happen before or during her period. These symptoms can include moodiness, sadness, anxiety, bloating, and acne. The symptoms go away after the first few days of a period.

What Can I Do About Cramps?

Many girls have cramps with their period, especially in the first few days. If cramps bother you, you can try:

a warm heating pad on your belly

taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin, or store brand) or naproxen (Aleve or store brand)

Should I Watch out for any Problems?

Most girls don't have any problems with their periods. Talk to an adult or see a doctor if you:

are 15 and haven't started your period

have had your period for more than 2 years and it still doesn't come regularly (about every 4–5 weeks)

Cramps are severe, and you seem to be bleeding between periods

have severe cramps that don't get better with ibuprofen or naproxen 

have very heavy bleeding (bleeding that goes through a pad or tampon faster than every 1 hour)

have periods that last more than about a week

It has been 3 months since your last period

have severe PMS that gets in the way of your everyday activities

Daily Checklist for a Changing body

  • Shower preferably twice a day or at least once a day
  • Clean vagina ONLY with fresh water, NO douching liquids or chemicals.
  • Use deodorant or anti- per spirant on the underarms
  • Wash face daily to help prevent acne
  • Brush teeth twice per day
  • Eat well balanced diets
  • Get plenty of exercise and rest
  • Do not wear under garments repeatedly, it is preferable to wash and dry them under the sun before wearing again.

2.4. HIV and other STIs
